In addition, general-purpose MCMC-based estimators such as path sampling have been proposed for SEMs (see Lee, 2007). In this paper, marginal likelihoods are estimated using bridge sampling (Gronau et al., 2017; Meng & Wong, 1996), as implemented in the bridgesampling package (Gronau et al., 2020). We use blavaan in combination with bridgesampling so that the approach applies broadly to SEMs specified in standard SEM syntax and can be replicated and extended without requiring a custom Stan implementation for each model variant (Stan Development Team, 2025). Technical requirements for obtaining bridge-sampling marginal likelihoods from fitted blavaan/Stan models are summarized in the appendix. All R code is provided in a Zenodo repository (see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23397657).

Unit-Information Priors for SEM Parameters

To establish a computational baseline that is closely connected to BIC-type Bayes factors, we construct explicit unit-information (UI) priors by using information from maximum likelihood (ML) fits. This baseline serves two functions: it approximates the BIC's implicit prior assumptions by an explicit prior, and it provides a controlled reference point for assessing the impact of incorporating additional prior information in later sections.

For each model, we fit the SEM using maximum likelihood estimation (ML) in the R-package lavaan (Rosseel, 2012) and extract the ML estimates and their estimated sampling covariance. Let θj denote the ML estimate of parameter θ j and let Var( θj ) denote the corresponding diagonal element of the ML covariance matrix. We define the UI variance for each parameter as where N is the sample size.

Intuitively, this scaling yields a dispersion corresponding to one observation's worth of information (Kass & Wasserman, 1995; Raftery, 1999; Weakliem, 1999). Because the ML estimates and their sampling covariance are computed from the same data that are subsequently compared, this construction is an empirical-Bayes device, a transparent analogue of the BIC, rather than a prior-to-data specification. Datadependent default priors are standard in objective Bayesian model comparison: intrinsic Bayes factors (Berger & Pericchi, 1996), fractional Bayes factors (O'Hagan, 1995), and the unit-information prior itself (Kass & Wasserman, 1995) all use the data to calibrate the prior. The double use of the data is concentrated in the UI baseline, which borrows both location (MLE centering) and scale from the data; the zero-centered variants introduced below remove the data-dependent centering for the focal parameters and retain only the data-dependent dispersion, that we regard as relatively diffuse.

Because blavaan by default expresses prior distributions through a set of univariate families, we implement the unit-information (UI) baseline in a parameter-wise way: each free parameter is assigned a univariate prior whose mean and variance match its UI targets, and the joint prior is taken as the product across parameters. Consequently, we do not attempt to reproduce the full UI prior covariance structure implied by the ML sampling covariance matrix; instead, the UI construction is implemented parameterwise to capture the intended "one-observation" informativeness for each free parameter. This strategy mirrors a simplified unit-information construction proposed by Ntzoufras (2009), who replaces the multivariate UI prior by independent priors with means equal to the posterior means under a flat (improper) prior and with variances equal to the corresponding posterior variances multiplied by N , yielding a convenient BIC-like baseline for model comparison.

The blavaan package provides a convenient set of priors tailored to common SEM parameter types, such that the distributional form is naturally matched to the parameter block: normal priors for loadings and regressions, gamma priors for variance-type parameters, and beta priors (after transformation) for correlations. Therefore we assign priors by parameter block (corresponding to free elements of Λ, B, Θ, and Ψ) and determine the associated hyperparameters by moment matching so that each prior attains its unit-information mean and variance targets. This yields a UI-prior baseline for the prior-sensitivity analyses and extensions considered in later sections.

For each free factor loading λ and structural regression coefficient β (i.e., free elements of Λ and B), we use a normal prior, where µ j equals either the ML estimate θj (UI-centering) or 0 in the zero-centered variants described below, and Var UI (θ j ) = N Var( θj ).

For variance-type parameters v j > 0 (free diagonal elements of Θ and, where applicable, Ψ), we assign a gamma prior to the variance itself (the [var] option in blavaan; the blavaan default is a gamma prior on the standard-deviation scale), with (a j , b j ) chosen by moment matching so that the prior mean equals the ML estimate vj and the prior variance equals the unit-information target N Var(v j ).

The latent variances (the diagonal of Ψ) are free parameters only in the simulation study, where the latent variables are identified by marker variables; in all other analyses the latent variables are identified by fixing their variances. For the latent variances we additionally bound the shape a j below at 0.5 while keeping the prior mean, because the unit-information approach can otherwise place most of the prior mass near zero. For each focal latent correlation ρ ∈ (-1, 1), we place a beta prior on the transformed parameter x = (ρ + 1)/2 ∈ (0, 1), where (a, b) are selected by matching the desired mean and unit-information variance of ρ (equivalently, of x).

In some cases, the UI-implied variance would correspond to a beta distribution with extreme or ill-behaved shape parameters. In those cases, we apply mild regularization in two steps. First, we re-express the beta parameters in terms of an "effective prior sample size" n 0 via a = xn 0 and b = (1 -x)n 0 (so that a+b = n 0 ). We then (i) cap n 0 at a moderate value (here n0 ≤ 10) to avoid excessively concentrated priors, and (ii) enforce unimodality by requiring a ≥ 1 and b ≥ 1, implemented by imposing a lower bound on n 0 that guarantees both inequalities given the target mean x. After applying these bounds, we set a and b from the bounded n 0 , which preserves the intended mean and yields a dispersion close to the UI target while ensuring a numerically stable beta prior. In practice, we have found that our regularization for the extreme cases often leads to a uniform distribution, that is, Beta(1, 1).

Because correlation matrices must be positive definite, the prior that blavaan samples need not coincide with the specified beta prior; in our analyses this affects only the datacentered UI baseline, not the zero-centered variants introduced below (see Appendix A.2).

In the present paper, we use blavaan with Stan to leverage Stan's efficient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling while retaining the convenience and reproducibility of standard SEM syntax. Our UI construction is therefore designed to operate within this fast Stan-based workflow: we translate unit-information targets into the prior families supported by blavaan/Stan and calibrate their hyperparameters by moment matching. This preserves the practical advantages of the blavaan-Stan pipeline while still yielding a unit-information baseline for the prior-sensitivity analyses that follow.

Reproducing BIC-Type Bayes Factors with UI Priors

In order to obtain the UI-type Bayes factors we fit the competing models in blavaan under the explicit UI priors and estimate their marginal likelihoods via bridge sampling, yielding log BF bridge 10

We also compute BIC-type Bayes factors via Equation (3) as a benchmark. In addition to the BIC approximation, we report a Laplace-type approximation to the marginal loglikelihood as an intermediate large-sample benchmark. In general, Laplace approximations are based on a second-order Taylor expansion of the log posterior around a central point, often the posterior mode (Kass & Raftery, 1995; Kass et al., 1991). In blavaan, this approximation is constructed around the posterior mean rather than the posterior mode. We include this quantity only as a diagnostic comparison alongside the BIC-based approximation and the bridge-sampling estimate.

UI-0: Zero-Centered Unit Information Priors for Focal Parameters

To isolate the effect of prior location on model comparison, we construct a zero-centered UI-variance variant. We identify a set of focal parameters that distinguish M 1 from M 0 (i.e., structural regressions and latent correlations that are free in M 1 but fixed to zero in M 0 ). For these focal parameters we replace the UI prior mean µ j = θj by µ j = 0 while keeping the UI variance unchanged:

In the extensions, this modification applies to the focal effects (regression and correlation coefficients) that are free in M 1 but fixed to 0 in M 0 , and analogously to any focal latent correlations that differ between models (implemented as beta priors centered at ρ = 0 after transformation). Non-focal priors follow the general convention stated above (see Table 1. This construction yields Bayes factors that differ from the UI baseline only through prior location on the focal structural relations.

UI-0-half: Zero-Centered Half-Width UI Priors for Focal Parameters

To assess sensitivity to the width of the focal priors, we define a half-width variant of UI-0.

As in UI-0, we center the focal structural relations at zero, but we halve their UI prior standard deviations. For focal loading and regression parameters this yields

For focal latent correlations, the same principle is applied on the transformed scale by re-calibrating the beta prior to retain zero centering (i.e., centering at ρ = 0) while halving the UI-type target standard deviation. Thus, UI-0-half differs from UI-0 only in the scale of the focal priors, allowing us to examine how strongly the Bayes factor depends on the amount of prior concentration around zero. Non-focal priors follow the same convention as UI-0.

UI-0-dir: Directional Zero-Centered Unit-Information Priors for Focal Parameters

Directional hypotheses are common in substantive SEM applications, where theory often predicts the sign of focal relations. Incorporating this information can sharpen model comparison by concentrating prior mass on theoretically plausible regions. In the Stanbased blavaan workflow used here, truncated priors (i.e., priors restricted to inequalityconstrained regions) are not conveniently supported in our bridge-blavaan workflow, and therefore we evaluate directional hypotheses using the encompassing-prior approach (Klugkist et al., 2005). 2Let C denote a set of order constraints on focal parameters, for instance where β is a latent regression coefficient and ρ is a latent correlation coefficient.

Let M e denote the unconstrained (encompassing) model and M c the corresponding constrained model. The constrained model M c is obtained by restricting the parameter space of M e to values that satisfy C. M c has the same likelihood as M e , but uses the encompassing prior truncated to C and renormalized. Let p(y | M e ) denote the marginal likelihood of the encompassing model under the chosen prior. The marginal likelihood of the constrained model M c can be obtained via the encompassing-prior approach as where Pr(C | M e ) is the prior probability mass that the encompassing prior assigns to the constrained region C, i.e., the integral of the encompassing prior over C; and Pr(C | y, M e ) is the corresponding posterior probability mass under the encompassing model.

In practice, we apply this adjustment on the log scale for numerical stability.

In the implementation, Pr(C | M e ) is estimated by MCMC draws from the joint prior distribution using blavaan's prior sampling option (prisamp=TRUE), and Pr(C | y, M e ) is estimated from posterior MCMC draws as the proportion of draws satisfying the constraints. Concretely, we fit the unconstrained model M e under the chosen prior, obtain prior draws from the same model, compute the prior and posterior constraint probabilities as proportions of draws satisfying C. In our applications, M e corresponds to the unconstrained version of the structural model M 1 ; hence the constrained comparison against M 0 is obtained by replacing p(y | M 1 ) with p(y | M c ) in the Bayes factor. Because the adjustment multiplies the marginal likelihood of the encompassing model, the twosided Bayes factor under the same prior is always available alongside the directional one; we recommend reporting both, so that it is transparent how much of the evidence stems from the directional restriction.

We estimate Pr(C | M e ) using blavaan's prior sampling option rather than by evaluating the constraint probability analytically or by sampling from separate univariate priors, because the constraints C are defined on the joint distribution of the focal parameters under the full SEM parameterization. Even when the user specifies seemingly independent priors on individual parameters, the effective prior on the model-implied latent covariance matrix is shaped by identification constraints, in particular the requirement of positive definiteness (for details, see Merkle et al., 2023). Prior sampling via blavaan therefore yields a direct Monte Carlo estimate of Pr(C | M e ) under exactly the same parameterization, transformations, and constraints used for posterior sampling and bridge sampling.

With this MCMC-based sampling strategy it is important to monitor how often the constrained region is visited. If only a tiny fraction of prior or posterior draws satisfy C, the Monte Carlo estimates of Pr(C | M e ) and/or Pr(C | y, M e ) can be unstable. Substantively, very small Pr(C | M e ) indicates that the encompassing prior assigns little mass to the hypothesized direction, suggesting a mismatch between the directional claim and the chosen prior parameterization; very small Pr(C | y, M e ) indicates that the data place little posterior mass in the constrained region. In either case, the first remedy is typically to reconsider the directional specification (e.g., by shifting or concentrating prior mass toward the theoretically expected region), rather than merely increasing the number of draws.

When the constrained region genuinely has very low probability but is still of interest, it can help to use estimators that are designed for inequality constraints rather than relying on the raw "fraction-of-draws" count. For example, Sarafoglou et al. (2023) provide a practical workflow for order-restricted hypotheses that replaces brute-force counting by a more efficient Monte Carlo strategy tailored to the constrained region. Another pragmatic alternative is to replace the raw proportion estimator by the result of fitting a parametric distribution to the prior and posterior draws (e.g., a multivariate normal on an unconstrained scale, or a copula-based model) and then estimating Pr(C | M e ) and Pr(C | y, M e ) under the fitted density.

In our extensions, if no draw satisfies the constraint, we do not treat the estimated probability as exactly zero; we use the rule-of-three upper bound (Hanley & Lippman-Hand, 1983; Jovanovic & Levy, 1997), 3/ESS, where ESS is the effective number of draws, and report the resulting Bayes factor as a bound. Regardless of the computational tactic that is employed, inspecting these probabilities remains useful because it reveals the extent to which the directional constraint is aligned with the prior and with the data.

Transparency and Openness

All materials needed to reproduce the results (model syntax, analysis scripts, simulation code, and the proxy dataset used in the extensions) are available in a Zenodo repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23397657; the repository also includes scripts to recreate the proxy dataset from the published summary statistics and to reproduce all analyses and results. Data were analyzed using R, version 4.5.2 (simulation study: version 4.5.1) (R Core Team, 2025); the detailed info about packages and simulation environments can be found in the Zenodo repository. This work was not preregistered. ChatGPT (GPT-5.2 Thinking; OpenAI) and Claude (Opus 5; Anthropic) were used for grammar checking, minor editing, programming support, and brainstorming during manuscript preparation; all decisions about content, analyses, and interpretation were made by the authors.

Simulation Study

This section explores the proposed methodology with a simulation study inspired by a real-data example from clinical psychology, focusing on structural relations that are typical of applied SEM research. Figure 2 depicts the five-factor SEM from the original study motivated by clinical theorizing about addictive behaviors and depressive symptoms. The measurement model comprises latent factors for addictive behaviors, depressive symptoms, childhood trauma, structural deficit, and despair, each indicated by multiple observed variables. The example is adapted from Fuchshuber et al. (2018), who analyzed data Addictive Behaviors Depressive Symptoms Structural Deficit Despair Childhood Trauma Problems Craving Frequency Expectations Concerns Failed Attempts Suicidal Thoughts Hopelessness Worthlessness Melancholy Loneliness Apathy Identity Diffusion Primitive Defense Reality Testing Seeking Sadness Emotional Abuse Physical Abuse Sexual Abuse Emotional Neglect Note. The figure is adapted from Fuchshuber et al. (2018). To simplify the analyses we removed the observed covariate 'Sex' predicting Addictive Behaviors and Depressive Symptoms from the original model.

from N = 500 German-speaking young adults (age: M = 26.0, SD = 5.51; 63.2% female) recruited online. In that study, addictive behaviors were assessed with symptom-class indicators (i.e., frequency, craving, problems, failed expectations, concerns, and failed attempts), depressive symptoms were assessed with six depression indicators (i.e., apathy, loneliness, melancholy, worthlessness, hopelessness, and suicidal thoughts), childhood trauma was indicated by four subscales (i.e., emotional neglect, sexual abuse, physical abuse, and emotional abuse), structural deficit was indicated by three subscales (i.e., identity diffusion, primitive defense, and reality testing), and despair was operationalized by two indicators (i.e., seeking and sadness). 3The structural component specifies a theoretically motivated mediation model in which ChildhoodTrauma is hypothesized to affect AddictiveBehaviors and DepressiveSymptoms directly and indirectly via StructuralDeficit and Despair (Fuchshuber et al., 2018). For the simulation study, we used a reduced version of this SEM that omits the weakly identified latent variable Despair. We compared two nested structural specifications that differ only in a small set of focal relations (Figure 3). The full model M 1 includes five structural relations, whereas the restricted model M 0 fixes three focal relations to zero: ChildhoodTrauma→StructuralDeficit, StructuralDeficit→AddictiveBehaviors, and the covariance AddictiveBehaviors↔DepressiveSymptoms. We emphasize that this fixed set of focal relations is chosen purely for illustration in a controlled simulation setting; in applied work, one would typically investigate the evidence for including each candidate path (or for competing path patterns) rather than focusing on a single preselected subset.

Our simulation study serves three purposes. First, it provides a fully controlled setting in which the data-generating model is known, allowing us to illustrate the complete priorto-Bayes-factor workflow. Second, it demonstrates how incorporating modest substantive information-here, simple directional expectations on focal structural relations-can improve model selection relative to a purely unit-information (BIC-like) baseline, which may otherwise favor overly simple structural specifications when the true model is comparatively complex. Third, because informative priors can also mislead, it examines their cost: we cross three data-generating conditions (M 1 true, M 1 true with halved focal effects, and M 0 true) with three sample sizes, so that the behavior of the priors can be assessed when the focal effects are weak or absent and not only when they are present.

Implementation

All analyses were conducted in R (see https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23397657 for the code). Maximum-likelihood fits were obtained with lavaan. For the BIC-based Bayes factors, we used the fitted lavaan objects to extract BIC values and obtained the BIC Bayes factor via Equation (3). For all other prior settings, the lavaan fits serve as the starting point for the UI-style prior construction described above. The resulting priors were encoded in blavaan model syntax, the corresponding Bayesian SEMs were fitted with blavaan, and marginal likelihoods were estimated from the MCMC output using bridgesampling with the warp-III bridge-sampling procedure (for details, see Gronau et al., 2020).

Unless noted otherwise, all Bayesian fits used four chains, discarded 1,000 warmup iterations per chain, and retained 4,000 post-warmup iterations per chain, yielding a total of 16,000 post-warmup draws. As an additional benchmark, we also report blavaan's built-in Laplace approximation to the log marginal likelihood for each fitted model under the corresponding prior specification. Thus, the Laplace approximation is evaluated separately for each prior condition (e.g., UI, UI-0), and can be compared directly to the bridge-sampling estimate obtained under that same model-and-prior setup.

For each prior condition, Bayes factors were obtained from differences in estimated log marginal likelihoods for the two competing models, optionally followed by an encompassingprior adjustment when directional order constraints are imposed. To limit the influence of poorly behaved estimation, only replications in which the maximum-likelihood fits converged successfully were retained. A Bayesian fit with divergent transitions or an effective-sample-size warning was refitted with a new seed, up to ten attempts; a replication whose fit still showed either problem after the tenth attempt was discarded, as was any Addictive Behaviors Depressive Symptoms Structural Deficit Childhood Trauma .2 (.1) .2 (.1) .5 .5 .1 (.05) Note. The population model fixes all factor loadings to λ = 0.7 and sets the corresponding indicator residual variances to θ = 1 -0.72 = 0.51. The structural part encodes standardized effects from ChildhoodTrauma to StructuralDeficit (β = 0.2), from ChildhoodTrauma and StructuralDeficit to AddictiveBehaviors (β = 0.5 and β = 0.2), and from StructuralDeficit to DepressiveSymptoms (β = 0.5), and includes a latent correlation between Addictive-Behaviors and DepressiveSymptoms (ρ = 0.1; see Figure 3). This M 1 -true condition is complemented by two data-generating conditions that differ only in the three focal effects: in the smaller-effect condition they are halved (β = 0.1 for both focal regressions and ρ = 0.05), and in the M 0 -true condition they are set to zero (the two focal regressions and the latent correlation are removed). The measurement model and the non-focal paths are identical across conditions, and the latent residual variances are adjusted so that the endogenous latent variables remain standardized.

In each replication we simulate N = 200, N = 500, or N = 1000 observations (one sample size per cell of the 3 × 3 design), fit the common measurement model, and compare M 1 versus M 0 as defined above and in Figure 3. All non-focal measurement and structural components are held constant across models. Latent factors are identified using marker-variable scaling (one loading per factor fixed to 1), and observed indicator means are fixed to zero in both models.

Each cell of the design is based on the first 1,000 valid replications (we ran 1,060, 1,040, and 1,030 replications per cell at N = 200, N = 500, and N = 1000, respectively, so that at least 1,000 valid ones remained after excluding failed and nonconverged ones). The cells were run in parallel on the Snellius supercomputer, on 100 workers for N = 200 and N = 500 and on 32 workers for N = 1000, and took between about 5 and 21 hours of wall-clock time each, which amounts to about 5,300 core-hours in total (wall-clock time multiplied by the number of workers).

We report the results in two steps: first, we assess the degree to which bridgesampled Bayes factors under unit-information priors reproduce the BIC-based Bayes factor approximation (Figure 4); second, we examine how changing the amount, location, and direction of prior information on the focal parameters (UI, UI-0, UI-0-half, and UI-0-dir) alters the evidence for the data-generating model M 1 relative to this baseline (Table 2). In the second step, we also report a "wrong-direction" variant (UI-0-dir (wrong)) in which the directional constraint is intentionally set opposite to the data-generating signs (i.e., it requires the focal regressions and the latent covariance to be negative). This condition is included purely as a sanity check: if the method behaves as intended, imposing a direction that contradicts the data-generating process should yield overwhelming evidence against the directional hypothesis, thereby illustrating how directional Bayes factors appropriately penalize substantively implausible (or misspecified) sign restrictions.

Results

Firstly, the results confirm that the bridge-sampled log Bayes factors under the UI-type priors closely track the log Bayes factors as obtained from the BIC approximation. Figure 4 shows, for each replication, the relationship between the BIC log Bayes factor (horizontal axis) and the corresponding bridge-sampled log Bayes factor under the UI prior (vertical axis), with separate panels for each cell of the design (data-generating conditions in columns, sample sizes in rows). Overall, the two approaches agree closely: in every cell, the points fall tightly along the line of equality, indicating that the bridge-sampled UI Bayes factors preserve the ordering and relative magnitude of the BIC Bayes factors (including replications with log BF10 < 0 at N = 200).

At the same time, the bridge-sampled UI log Bayes factors tend to be slightly larger than their BIC counterparts, as reflected by the mild upward displacement of the point cloud relative to the equality line. This small disparity is expected: the BIC Bayes factor relies on a large-N Laplace approximation under a specific implicit unit-information prior, whereas bridge sampling evaluates the marginal likelihood under the exact UI prior used in our fits. Because our UI prior is implemented as a product of univariate, block-specific priors, it is generally not identical to the multivariate normal unit-information prior that is implicit in the standard BIC/Laplace derivation. One reason is the prior on the bounded latent residual correlation: a Beta prior cannot be as dispersed as the unit-information variance of this parameter requires (in our implementation its shape parameters are bounded below by one, so it is at most uniform), which makes it more concentrated than the corresponding normal prior and can therefore raise the log marginal likelihood of M 1 . Hence, even aside from asymptotic error, small systematic differences between the BIC approximation and bridge-sampled UI Bayes factors can arise.

Secondly, the results show that the Bayes factor is influenced primarily by adding directional information (UI-0-dir) and by halving the prior standard deviation (UI-0-half). Table 2 summarizes the resulting values of log BF true , the log Bayes factor in favor of the data-generating model, across replications for the three data-generating conditions and N = 200, N = 500, and N = 1000, reporting its mean and the proportion of replications in which BF true exceeds the conventional threshold of 3 (Appendix B adds the thresholds 1 and 10).

For M 1 true and N = 200, the standard UI-based conditions (BIC, UI, UI-LA, and UI-0) yield moderate evidence for the true model M 1 . In particular, bridge-sampled Bayes factors under the UI prior are slightly larger than those based on the BIC approximation, with the Laplace approximation (UI-LA) falling in between. Centering only the focal parameters at zero while retaining the UI dispersion (UI-0) does not materially affect the results, again suggesting that prior location is less consequential than prior scale. In contrast, halving the prior standard deviation for the focal parameters (UI-0-half) noticeably strengthens the evidence, increasing both the mean log Bayes factor and the proportion of replications with at least moderate support for M 1 (e.g., Pr(BF10 > 3) =0.697). Imposing the correct directional constraint via the encompassing-prior adjustment (UI-0-dir) yields the largest gain, with mean(log BF10 ) =4.22 and Pr(BF10 > 3) =0.730.

For M 1 true and N = 500 and N = 1000, all methods strongly favor the true model, indicating that the data are sufficiently informative for the comparison to become decisive regardless of the prior specification. Nevertheless, the same ordering remains visible: UI exceeds BIC slightly, UI-0 remains close to UI, and both UI-0-half and especially UI-0-dir further strengthen the evidence. As a negative control, applying the directional constraint in the wrong direction sharply reduces the support for M 1 : where no posterior draw satisfied the constraint, its Bayes factor can only be bounded, at about 6.5 log units below the corresponding UI-0 value (the numbers of such replications are given in the notes to Tables B.1 and B.2). The robust mixture priors of Extension I are designed to guard against this failure mode.

When the focal effects are smaller, the evidence accumulates more slowly, as expected for an evidence measure that weighs the support for the effects against the added complexity. At N = 200 and N = 500, the mean log Bayes factor in favor of M 1 is negative under every method, so the simpler model is typically favored; at N = 1000 the mean turns positive. The informative priors shift the evidence toward M 1 at every sample size: at N = 1000, BF10 > 3 in 0.630 (UI-0-half) and 0.673 (UI-0-dir) of the replications, compared with 0.471 under BIC. Effects of this size thus require a lot of data to be detected, which marks a limit of the workflow, but it also means that the Bayes factor does not lend support to very small effects, which may be negligible in practice.

When M 0 is true, all methods favor the simpler model in almost all replications (Pr(BF true > 3) ≥ 0.977 in every cell), and the evidence strengthens with N (mean log BF01 under UI-0 of 5.93, 7.26, and 8.29). The informative priors do not manufacture evidence for the absent effects: UI-0-half gives the least evidence for M 0 (mean log BF01 = 4.57 at N = 200, compared with 6.45 for BIC), whereas UI-0-dir gives the most (7.11).

Overall, these results highlight a common problem: when the data are only moderately informative, default large-sample approximations such as BIC (and closely related unitinformation baselines) may yield Bayes factors that are comparatively weak and therefore less decisive for selecting among substantively distinct structural models. Moreover, because the BIC penalty grows with the number of free parameters, it can be especially conservative in complex settings such as SEM, where comparatively rich models are easily penalized even when they capture genuine (but moderately large) effects. In contrast, modest and theory-consistent prior refinements can substantially sharpen the comparison. 4In our simulation, reducing the dispersion of the focal priors (UI-0-half) increases the frequency of strong evidence for the data-generating model, and incorporating directional expectations (UI-0-dir) strengthens the evidence further when the imposed direction is correct.

At the same time, the UI-type prior remains useful as an explicit analogue of the BIC baseline that can be deployed in sensitivity analyses -providing a principled reference point against which to assess the impact of adding substantive prior information. We next turn to extensions that mirror this workflow in an empirical setting.

The simulation does not address model misspecification. Because a Bayes factor is conditional on the models being compared, we recommend checking proactively whether the models reproduce the data at all, for example with a landscape analysis (Navarro et al., 2004) (Appendix A.3); we do so for the real data in Extension I (Figure 5).

Extensions

We illustrate the proposed blavaan-bridge workflow in a realistic SEM framework that explicitly addresses prior sensitivity and model uncertainty, by (I) combining robust mixture priors for focal structural relations with Bayesian model comparison and (II) Bayesian model averaging (BMA) across a set of competing structural specifications.

We return to the Depression model of Fuchshuber et al. (2018) and, in contrast to the reduced simulation example, consider the full specification, that is, including the latent factor Despair (see Figure 2). Because the original paper does not provide the raw dataset but reports the empirical means, standard deviations, and correlation matrix for the observed indicators, we recreate an empirical proxy dataset (N = 500) by sampling from a multivariate normal distribution whose moment structure matches the published

We use this proxy Depression dataset for two applied demonstrations. First, we show how robust mixture priors can be implemented in Bayesian SEM within our UI-type prior construction framework. Second, we use the same dataset to illustrate Bayesian model averaging (BMA) over a set of competing structural specifications: we evaluate candidate models using bridge sampling (after pruning the model space), and then perform BMA to address model selection uncertainty in a principled manner.

Extension I: Robust Mixture Priors

Since we wish to compare two models under different priors, we first check whether they are adequate models of the data at all, because a Bayes factor is conditional on the models being compared and cannot reveal that both of them fit poorly. We use a landscape analysis (Navarro et al., 2004): datasets are generated from each model after it has been fitted to the data (a parametric bootstrap; Wagenmakers et al., 2004), every generated dataset is scored under both models by its marginal likelihood as approximated by the BIC, and the marginal likelihood of the observed data (via BIC) are located among the generated ones. Data that lie far outside the resulting clouds are not representative of either model. The implementation is described in Appendix A.3; the result for the present data is reported at the beginning of the Results below.

The choice of prior for structural relations can have a substantial impact on Bayes factors. To mitigate sensitivity to any single specification and lessen the potential for data-prior conflict, we consider robust mixture priors that average two prior components (e.g., Berger et al., 1994; Bose, 1994; Macrì Demartino et al., in press; Wagenmakers and Matzke, 2024). Let π 1 (θ) and π 2 (θ) denote two candidate priors for the parameter vector θ under the same structural model M 1 . We define the mixture prior where w ∈ [0, 1] is a mixing weight set by the analyst.

The corresponding marginal likelihood is the mixture of marginal likelihoods, 5 Concretely, we omit Sex and use the remaining reported means and standard deviations together with the corresponding submatrix of the reported correlation matrix to form the covariance matrix Σ = diag(s) R diag(s).

We then generate multivariate data with these moments and standardize the variables, yielding a dataset that reproduces the target correlation matrix by construction. Furthermore, in the original study, Seeking loaded negatively on the Despair factor. To align the measurement direction of both indicators and to facilitate more stable posterior sampling in blavaan, we reverse-scored Seeking such that higher values indicate more despair.

In the present application, θ denotes the vector of focal structural parameters (i.e., the structural paths that are free in M 1 and fixed to zero in M 0 ). The first component, π 1 , is a vague baseline prior for these focal relations: we use the UI-0 specification (zero-centered unit-information priors on the focal regressions) together with blavaan defaults for nonfocal parameters. The second component, π 2 , is a more informative directional prior: it combines (i) reduced prior standard deviation for the focal relations (UI-0-half) with (ii) positivity constraints imposed via the encompassing-prior approach (UI-0-dir), yielding a UI-0-half-dir specification. Concretely, we evaluate the directional component by treating the UI-0-half prior as an encompassing prior and applying the standard adjustment based on prior and posterior mass in C, with C denoting the set of order constraints on the focal parameters (e.g., all focal effects are positive; see Subsection "UI-0-dir" for details).

This mixture specification guards against undue sensitivity to a single informative directional prior. In our application we use an equal-weight mixture (w = 0.5), so that the evidence reflects a balanced compromise between a vague baseline and theoretical expectations. More generally, the weights encode the analyst's confidence in the directional expectation: the more confident the analyst is about the sign, the more weight 1 -w is placed on the directional component π 2 , and moderate confidence corresponds to an intermediate weight such as w = 0.5. Intuitively, when posterior mass concentrates in the region emphasized by the directional half-variance prior, the marginal likelihood increases; when the theoretical expectations are not supported, the vague baseline component limits the penalty from potentially misspecified directionality. In this way, the mixture yields a comparison that is informative about the presence of the effects while remaining conservative with respect to their assumed direction. When the analyst has greater prior confidence in the expected direction and scale of the focal relations, the weight on the informative prior component may be increased accordingly.

In our example, we compare two structural specifications that share the same measurement model (Figure 2). The full model M 1 freely estimates all structural paths, whereas the restricted model M 0 fixes the following four direct effects to zero: (1) Addic-tiveBehaviors~Despair, (2) AddictiveBehaviors~ChildhoodTrauma, (3) DepressiveSymp-toms~ChildhoodTrauma, and (4) DepressiveSymptoms~StructuralDeficit; all remaining (non-focal) measurement and structural components are held identical across M 1 and M 0 . These four paths represent direct effects in a mediation setting, which theory may predict to be positive but comparatively small relative to the indirect (mediated) pathways. This is precisely the kind of situation in which a robust mixture prior is useful: it allows us to encode a weak directional expectation for the direct effects while retaining an "insurance" component that protects the Bayes factor against data-prior conflict, that is, the possibility that one or more direct effects are effectively absent or even negative.

Implementation

In our analysis, y is the N = 500 proxy dataset described above. For all applied analyses we identify the latent variables using factor-variance scaling (std.lv = TRUE) rather than marker-variable scaling. That is, each latent variance is fixed to one and all factor loadings are freely estimated. In our experience with the present models, this parameterization yields more stable MCMC behavior than marker scaling.foot_4 Our implementation follows the same workflow as described above: we use lavaan for initial maximum-likelihood fits, translate the resulting UI-type priors into blavaan syntax, and fit the Bayesian SEMs in blavaan. Unless noted otherwise, we run four chains with 1,000 warmup iterations and 4,000 post-warmup iterations per chain. Marginal likelihoods are estimated via bridge sampling using the bridgesampling R package, and Bayes factors are computed from differences in estimated log marginal likelihoods; we report results only for fits that converged without substantive MCMC warnings (e.g., divergent transitions or low effective sample sizes). On a standard computer (Apple silicon, 8 cores; the four chains run in parallel), each bridge-sampled fit took between 1.9 and 3.9 minutes, and the complete analysis, including the prior sampling for the directional Bayes factors, took about 10 minutes.

Results

In the landscape analysis, Figure 5 shows that the proxy data lie in the middle of both clouds: 47.6% of the datasets generated from the fitted M 1 fit worse under M 1 than the proxy data do, and 43.1% of those generated from the fitted M 0 fit worse under M 0 . Neither model is thus contradicted by the covariance structure of the data.

Our results show a clear pattern. Under the vague insurance prior for the focal direct effects (i.e., UI-0 with blavaan default priors on the non-focal parameters), the bridgesampled Bayes factor strongly favors the restricted model (M 0 ), BF10 = 4.73 × 10 -5 (equivalently, BF01 = 21,140.47), indicating that the data offer overwhelming support for excluding the four focal direct paths under scrutiny.

The analysis using the width-reduced directional specification (UI-0-half-dir) yields a similar conclusion. First, halving the prior standard deviation without imposing directionality (UI-0-half) yields BF10 = 7.20 × 10 -4 (equivalently, BF01 = 1,388.86), benefiting M 1 by a factor of 15.22 relative to the vague UI-0 prior-close to the theoretically expected 24 = 16, since halving the standard deviation of a zero-centered normal doubles its density at zero for each of the four focal parameters. Under the UI-0-half encompassing prior, the positivity-constraint probability decreases from Pr(C | M 1 ) = 0.0632 to Pr(C | y, M 1 ) = 0.0134, which decreases the support for M 1 by a factor of approximately 4.73 (the ratio of the two probabilities before rounding), resulting in an encompassingadjusted Bayes factor of BF10 = 1.52 × 10 -4 (equivalently, BF01 = 6,562.70). Finally, the robust mixture prior yields BF10 = 9.98 × 10 -5 (equivalently, BF01 = 10,016.08), reflecting a compromise between the vague insurance component (UI-0) and the width-reduced directional component (UI-0-half-dir). Overall, across all prior specifications, the substantive conclusion is the same: the data overwhelmingly favor omitting the four direct paths.

Extension II: Bayesian Model Averaging

Bayesian model averaging (BMA) addresses a pervasive challenge in SEM: even when the measurement model is held fixed, the structural part induces an extremely large model space because many paths can be fixed or freed independently, often leaving the data compatible with a range of rival specifications rather than a single dominant one. In such settings, the common two-step workflow-first selecting a 'best-fitting' model and then conditioning all inference on that selection-creates model myopia: uncertainty from the selection stage is discarded, which can yield overly confident conclusions about which structural relations are present and about their estimated magnitude (e.g., Hoeting et al., 1999; MacCallum & Austin, 2000; Madigan & Raftery, 1994b; Wagenmakers et al., 2021 Wagenmakers et al., , 2022)). BMA addresses this problem by integrating model comparison and estimation: Rather than committing completely to a single winner, BMA propagates structural uncertainty by weighting each candidate model's contribution by its posterior model probability, that is, by updating prior model probabilities with each model's marginal likelihood (Raftery & Zheng, 2003; Wrinch & Jeffreys, 1921). This procedure yields model-averaged parameter estimates and predictions that are typically more stable and appropriately cautious when several structural explanations are competitive (Hinne et al., 2020). The strategy is closely aligned with the DAG-focused Bayesian model averaging approach of Kaplan and Lee (2016), who demonstrate how approximate Bayes factors can be used to navigate large structural model spaces and to summarize evidence via posterior model probabilities.

Let {M k } K k=1 denote a set of K candidate structural models that share the same measurement model but differ in which focal structural relations are freely estimated versus fixed to zero. Given marginal likelihoods p(y | M k ) and prior model probabilities p(M k ), the posterior model probabilities are determined by

Standard Bayesian model averaging (BMA) combines inference across these models by averaging a quantity of interest ∆ with respect to the posterior model probabilities. However, the marginal likelihoods-and consequently the weights p(M k | y)-depend on the specific choice of prior distributions for the model parameters. To prevent substantive conclusions from being contingent on a single prior specification, we extend the averaging framework to include uncertainty regarding the prior itself. Let {π s } S s=1 denote a set of plausible prior specifications (e.g., varying in dispersion or directionality), each assigned a prior probability p(π s ).

In the present application we set S = 4 and consider four focal-prior variants, all of them with blavaan default priors on the non-focal parameters. First, UI-0 serves as a baseline that encodes little information about the focal structural relations beyond symmetry around zero (i.e., it does not favor either direction and retains a relatively diffuse unit-information dispersion). Second, UI-0-half is a more informative variant that reflects the expectation that effects are unlikely to be large. Third, UI-0-dir incorporates directional information by imposing positivity constraints on the focal relations via the encompassing-prior approach under the UI-0 specification. Fourth, UI-0-half-dir combines both restrictions by imposing the same positivity constraints under the UI-0-half specification (i.e., with reduced focal prior variance).

The 'grand' posterior distribution of ∆ is then obtained by averaging over both the structural models and the prior settings: where p(M k , π s | y) is the joint posterior probability of model M k and prior specification π s .

This formulation results in a comprehensive mixture distribution that propagates uncertainty from both the structural specification and the prior shape into the inference stage.

In realistic SEM settings, the number of candidate models K can be very large because each candidate structural relation may be either included or fixed to zero, resulting in an exponential growth of the model set. For the model in Figure 2, there are m = 10 candidate structural relations, yielding K = 2 m = 1024 structural submodels. In many applications, theory can be used to restrict attention to a smaller, substantively motivated subset of models, but such preselection risks overlooking plausible alternatives. Rather than committing to a hand-picked subset, we use a two-stage strategy: a fast BIC-based Occam-window screening step to identify a small set of high-support candidates (Kaplan & Lee, 2016; Madigan & Raftery, 1994b), followed by fully Bayesian refitting of the selected candidates to obtain posterior model probabilities via bridge-sampled marginal likelihoods.

Implementation

We apply our analysis procedure to the same Depression proxy dataset that was introduced earlier. We first fit the fully specified structural model by maximum likelihood in lavaan using factor-variance identification (std.lv=TRUE) and screen the downward space of nested submodels using a BIC-based search. We traverse the tree of submodels obtained by fixing candidate latent regressions and covariances to zero, and we expand a model (i.e., evaluate its descendants) only if its BIC lies within an Occam window of the best BIC encountered so far. Following Kaplan and Lee (2016) we set C = 20, so models are expanded only when ∆BIC ≤ 2 log(20) ≈ 6 relative to the current best model; under the BIC approximation, this corresponds to excluding models that are worse than roughly 20 : 1 in Bayes-factor terms compared to the current best model. Models outside this window are not expanded, and their descendants are not explored. To assess the impact of this screening rule, we also exhaustively fit the full model space (which is feasible here; 210 = 1024 models). We found the highest-ranked models to be identical across the screened and exhaustive search.

When the window constant C is chosen to be relatively lenient, this set can still be larger than is practical for full Bayesian refitting. We therefore add a second screening phase, in which the BIC values from the models that survived the first screening phase are used to compute approximate posterior model probabilities under a uniform model prior; we then retain the smallest subset whose cumulative approximate posterior mass reaches 99%. This second screening step acts as a simple size control: it keeps the Bayesian refitting stage focused on a small number of high-support candidates (often only a handful) while discarding models that collectively carry negligible BIC-implied weight.

We then refit each retained model in blavaan under each of the four prior settings (UI-0, UI-0-half, UI-0-dir, UI-0-half-dir, with blavaan default priors on the non-focal parameters), using four MCMC chains with 1,000 warmup iterations and 4,000 post-warmup iterations per chain. Marginal likelihoods are estimated via warp-III bridge sampling in the bridgesampling R package, and posterior model probabilities are computed from these marginal likelihoods assuming equal prior probabilities over the retained models. On the same computer as in Extension I, the BIC-based screen evaluated 187 of the 1,024 possible models in about 15 seconds, and the Bayesian refits of the five retained models took about 30 minutes in total (roughly 6 minutes per model: two bridge-sampled fits, which took 2.4 minutes on average and 5.2 at most, and two prior-sampling runs of about half a minute each); the complete analysis took about 36 minutes.

To obtain the final prior-averaged BMA summaries, we assign equal prior weights to the four prior settings and compute posterior weights as proportional to p(y | M k , π s ) p(M k ) p(π s ). Model-averaged posterior parameter distributions are then formed as a mixture over (k, s): for symmetric priors, we use posterior draws directly from the fitted models; for the directional setting, we retain only draws satisfying the inequality constraints (rejection sampling from the encompassing posterior). Parameters fixed to zero in a given model contribute a point mass at zero. This produces grand-mixture posterior summaries that jointly reflect structural and prior uncertainty.

Results

The BMA workflow was applied to the depression example to identify the most plausible structural relations among the candidate paths. The initial Occam's window pruning (with window constant C = 20) reduced the full model space to a small set of high-support candidates; applying the 99% cumulative-mass rule to the resulting BIC-implied posterior weights yielded five models that were carried forward for Bayesian refitting. Table 3 details the structural specifications of these five models, while Table 4 presents their posterior model probabilities (PMP) across the four prior settings.

The table displays the five best models identified after BIC-based pruning with C = 20. ✓indicates that the structural path is freely estimated. The table structure is adapted from Boehm et al. (2024).

The results highlight the sensitivity of model selection to the specification of the prior parameter distribution (Table 4). Under the two symmetric priors (UI-0 and UI-0-half), the leading support is split between M 1 and M 2 , with a slight advantage for M 2 (PMPs: 0.467 and 0.416) over M 1 (PMPs: 0.428 and 0.382). Incorporating directional information shifts support toward the more complex model: under UI-0-dir and UI-0-half-dir, M 1 receives most of the posterior mass (PMPs: 0.514 and 0.490), whereas M 2 drops to 0.373 and 0.251. Thus, the directional priors favor including the residual correlation between AddictiveBehaviors and DepressiveSymptoms. The Monte Carlo uncertainty of the directional adjustment is small: across the five models and the two directional priors, the standard errors of the two constraint probabilities, based on the effective number of draws (at least 4,324 and 5,851, respectively), are at most 0.0027 and 0.0064.

When we average across all four prior settings with equal weights, M 1 emerges as the highest-ranked model (PMP = 0.453), followed by M 2 (PMP = 0.377). The corresponding Bayes factor, derived from the prior-averaged posterior model probabilities, is modest (BF12 = 1.20), indicating that the evidence distinguishing M 1 from M 2 is virtually nonexistent and that substantial model uncertainty remains regarding the inclusion of the residual correlation between AddictiveBehaviors and DepressiveSymptoms. Note. 'UI-0-half-dir' combines the halved standard deviation with the directional prior condition. PMP = Posterior Model Probability. 'Averaged Results' represent the weighted average across the four prior specifications (assuming equal prior weights). BF 1k is the Bayes factor comparing the best model (M 1 ) to model k, derived directly from the averaged posterior model probabilities. Models are sorted by their prior-averaged posterior probability.

Table 5 summarizes the BMA estimates for the structural paths, averaged across all retained models and prior settings. Five structural relations have an inclusion probability of 1 because they are present in all models that survived the BIC-based screening step. Thus, within the retained model space, these relations are treated as certain. For instance, the path DepressiveSymptoms~Despair shows a strong positive effect (Mean = 0.904, 95% HDI [0.831, 0.961]; HDI = highest posterior density interval).

In contrast, the residual correlation AddictiveBehaviors~~DepressiveSymptoms had an inclusion probability of 0.453, mirroring the uncertainty observed in the model comparison. Its unconditional posterior mean is therefore small (0.079) due to shrinkage, and its 95% HDI [0.000, 0.284] reflects the bi-modality of the posterior, that is, a mixture of a continuous effect under M 1 and a point mass at zero under the remaining retained models. The corresponding inclusion Bayes factor is 3.32, indicating modest evidence in favor of including this residual correlation. Among the remaining candidate paths, DepressiveSymptoms~ChildhoodTrauma is not strongly supported, but neither is it decisively ruled out (inclusion probability = 0.125; inclusion BF = 0.57). AddictiveBehav-iors~ChildhoodTrauma is less supported (inclusion probability = 0.040; inclusion BF = 0.17). The other candidate paths receive essentially no support.

Overall, the results from this example underscore the value of model averaging. Model comparison did not yield a single dominant structural specification: although M 1 and M 2 carry most of the posterior mass, the remaining retained models also contribute non-negligibly. The Bayes factor between M 1 and M 2 is close to one, indicating that the data provide little guidance for deciding whether the residual correlation between Addic-tiveBehaviors and DepressiveSymptoms should be included. In such settings, conditioning inference on only the top-ranked model would be misleading. BMA instead propagates this uncertainty, which is reflected directly in the posterior inclusion probabilities of the contested relations and in their model-averaged posterior distributions, some of which take the form of spike-and-slab mixtures, that is, a point mass at zero combined with a continuous component.

Posterior model probabilities depend on the marginal likelihood and therefore on the prior parameter distribution; accordingly, Table 4 shows that support for the leading models varies somewhat across plausible prior specifications. By averaging across the four priors considered here with equal weights, we obtain model and parameter summaries that are less contingent on any single prior choice. Conceptually, this prior-averaged BMA amounts to averaging over an expanded space that includes both structural specifications and prior settings, thereby propagating uncertainty about both.

Concluding Comments

The BIC is a common and convenient tool for model selection in structural equation modeling. Its popularity is understandable: it is available by default in SEM software, cheap to compute, and provides a simple penalty-based trade-off between fit and complexity. At the same time, BIC is only an asymptotic approximation to Bayesian model comparison. In particular, its Bayes-factor interpretation rests on a specific, implicit unit-information parameter prior that is effectively fixed by the approximation: researchers do not have a practical way to modify this prior to reflect substantive knowledge (e.g., plausible effect sizes, or directional expectations about focal paths). Moreover, the BIC-Bayes-factor link is accurate only up to an O(1) prior-dependent constant that can matter in finite samples. As a consequence, BIC-based conclusions can be sensitive to sample size and can understate model uncertainty, especially in SEM settings where models can be complex, sample sizes can be modest, and signals may be weak.

The goal of this paper was to make marginal-likelihood-based evidence measures (i.e., Bayes factors and posterior model probabilities) practical and transparent for SEM users, while retaining the flexibility to incorporate substantive prior information about latent relations. We pursued this goal in three steps. First, we constructed an explicit unitinformation (UI) prior from maximum-likelihood fits and estimated marginal likelihoods via bridge sampling. This "UI baseline" approximates BIC's prior assumptions by an explicit prior and provides a controlled reference point for sensitivity analyses. Second, we showed how the UI baseline can be sharpened by incorporating modest substantive prior information about focal structural relations, both by reducing the prior scale (UI-0-half) and by imposing directional expectations via an encompassing-prior adjustment (UI-0-dir), yielding more decisive evidence when these assumptions are appropriate. Third, we illustrated how these tools naturally extend to applied workflows: robust mixture priors and Bayesian model averaging (BMA) across a large set of structural submodels.

Across the simulation and extensions, two messages emerge. The first is methodological: bridge sampling combined with blavaan provides a broadly applicable route to marginal likelihoods for SEMs specified in standard syntax, so that Bayes factors become available without bespoke Stan coding; moreover, this workflow is not tied to UI-type priors and can be used with any proper prior supported by blavaan, including weakly informative and substantively elicited specifications. The second is substantive: prior specification matters for marginal-likelihood-based comparisons, but this sensitivity can be made informative rather than problematic. By explicitly stating and varying priors for focal relations-rather than relying on an implicit default-researchers can assess robustness, encode expectations when warranted, and quantify how much such assumptions sharpen or weaken the inferences. In the BMA setting, this same machinery yields posterior inclusion probabilities and model-averaged parameter summaries that propagate structural uncertainty instead of conditioning on a single selected model.

LOO, WAIC, and posterior predictive checks, discussed in the Introduction, complement Bayes factors in this workflow. Because a Bayes factor is conditional on the candidate model set, it cannot show that all candidate models fit poorly. A natural workflow is therefore to assess model adequacy first, for instance with posterior predictive checks or the landscape analysis used in Extension I (Appendix A.3), and then to use Bayes factors to compare the models that adequately describe the data.

Although our simulation focused on nested comparisons, the workflow is not restricted to them: bridge sampling estimates each model's marginal likelihood separately, so Bayes factors for non-nested models are obtained in the same way. What changes is the correspondence with BIC, which is better behaved for nested models (Kass & Wasserman, 1995); for non-nested comparisons we expect it to be looser, which strengthens the case for estimating marginal likelihoods directly. The prior variants must also be reinterpreted, because there is no focal parameter set that is free in one model and fixed to zero in the other. Zero-centering, dispersion-halving, and directional constraints can be applied to the structural relations within each model about which the analyst holds the corresponding expectation, and should be applied symmetrically across models unless genuinely asymmetric substantive knowledge warrants otherwise. The unit-information construction helps here, because it calibrates each prior to one observation's worth of information and thereby places both models on a common, data-calibrated scale.

For applied use, computing cost is modest. An analysis requires only a handful of fits, each of which takes a few minutes on a standard computer when the chains run in parallel (Extensions I and II took about 10 and 36 minutes in total); the fits are independent and can be parallelized further, and the posterior sample size can be reduced when the bridge-sampling error is small. The number of candidate models grows exponentially with the number of candidate structural paths, which is why a screening step restricts Bayesian refitting to a small set of high-support models. For substantially larger models, fitting time and memory, which grow with the number of indicators, free parameters, and posterior sample size, rather than the stability of the bridge-sampling estimate, are the practical constraints.

Three limitations are worth noting. First, although the encompassing-prior approach offers a practical solution for directional hypotheses in software that does not support truncation directly, it requires stable estimation of constraint probabilities and may become computationally inefficient when the constrained region has very small prior or posterior mass; in such cases, more specialized estimators for order-constrained hypotheses may be preferable (e.g., Sarafoglou et al., 2023). Second, full model-space exploration remains computationally challenging for large SEMs; our screening strategy uses BIC only as a pragmatic pruning device, after which final inference is fully Bayesian. Because the screen is based on BIC, it does not take the targeted priors into account, so a discarded model could in principle be favored by them. As a rough guide, relative to its value under the zero-centered unit-information prior (UI-0), a targeted prior can raise a model's marginal likelihood by a factor of at most about 4 k for k focal parameters (2 k from correct directional constraints and 2 k from halving the focal prior scale), so models somewhat outside the window cannot be ruled out. This is only a heuristic, and does not provide guarantees. In larger model spaces, where exhaustive checking is infeasible, screening based on the target priors themselves, for example Savage-Dickey density ratios computed from a single fit of the full model under multivariate-normal or Gaussian-copula approximations, may be preferable. Fast approximate Bayesian methods such as the INLAvaan package (Jamil & Rue, 2026) may make such screens practical, which we leave to future research; we have not evaluated them here. In settings where theory strongly restricts the candidate set, researchers may prefer to define a smaller set of substantively motivated models and apply the same bridge-sampling and BMA tools to that curated model space. Third, no simulation can cover every condition. Ours used one SEM structure, standardized loadings fixed at 0.7, and normally distributed indicators, so the results need not carry over to other structures, weaker measurement, or nonnormal data. In particular, nonnormality that leaves the covariance structure unchanged is invisible both to the normal-likelihood workflow and to the covariance-based landscape analysis (Appendix A.3).

Overall, the workflow developed here (Figure 1) aims to bring Bayesian evidence measures closer to routine SEM practice: (i) start from a baseline connected to BIC, (ii) introduce targeted and interpretable prior information for focal structural relations, (iii) compute marginal likelihoods via bridge sampling, and (iv) propagate model uncertainty through posterior model probabilities and BMA when many candidates are plausible. We hope this combination of accessibility, transparency, and flexibility will help SEM researchers move from single-model confirmation toward cumulative evidence assessment for structural hypotheses. free (i.e., an unrestricted block), blavaan may assign a single LKJ prior to that block rather than separate beta priors to its entries. In our setting, this can occur even when the analyst conceptually thinks in terms of a single "residual correlation": if that correlation appears as part of an unrestricted 2 × 2 sub-block within a larger correlation structure, it may be absorbed into a blockwise LKJ prior. If the block is only partly free, blavaan instead retains the beta priors in the parameter table, but warns that the actual prior may differ from the stated prior, since the positive-definiteness constraint still applies (Merkle et al., 2023).

When blavaan switches from beta to LKJ at the block level, it sets the LKJ shape parameter using the first beta prior it encounters for a parameter in that correlation matrix. For example, if the first encountered prior is Beta(4, 1), blavaan assigns LKJ(4) to the corresponding block; if the first encountered prior is Beta(1, 1), it assigns LKJ(1), which is uniform over correlation matrices. For a single correlation, that is, a 2 × 2 block, LKJ(a) is the symmetric Beta(a, a) on (-1, 1). This behavior implies that a correlation-specific beta prior may not be applied literally when the relevant correlations are part of an unrestricted block.

Figure A.1 illustrates this behavior. We placed an informative Beta(4, 1) prior, which concentrates mass near ρ = +1 (prior mean 0.6), on each of the three correlations among three latent variables, so that they form an unrestricted 3 × 3 block, and we sampled the joint prior with the prior-sampling option of blavaan (prisamp = TRUE). The sampled marginals are symmetric about zero (means of 0.00) and bear little resemblance to the specified density: the beta priors were replaced by an LKJ(4) prior on the block, which discards the specified location. Such a prior, which places most of its mass on high correlations, is also poorly suited to sampling.

Further details on how blavaan handles correlation-matrix priors and positive-definiteness constraints are described in Merkle et al. (2023). For our purposes, this behavior is usually not consequential. The UI-type priors in the main text are intended primarily as a weakly informative baseline that mimics the role of BIC's implicit unit-information prior, rather than as finely tuned priors for individual correlations. In that context, replacing correlation-specific beta priors by a weakly informative LKJ prior on the corresponding block typically preserves the intended role of the UI baseline while improving coherence with the positive-definite constraint.

Concretely, latent covariances enter our analyses as a focal parameter in the simulation, as non-focal parameters with blavaan's default prior in Extension I (where the focal parameters are regressions), and as candidate paths in the model-averaging analysis. Each forms its own 2 × 2 block, so the sampled prior is the symmetric Beta(a, a); the zero-centered variants (UI-0, UI-0-half, UI-0-dir) specify exactly such priors and are therefore unaffected, whereas only the data-centered UI baseline loses its centering on these parameters.

If correlation-specific UI-like beta priors are required, there are two options, neither of which is fully satisfactory. First, one can switch to the JAGS backend of blavaan (target = "jags"), which allows fully custom priors on individual correlations at the cost of F1~~F2 F1~~F3 F2~~F3 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 ρ Density Note. Red lines show the specified Beta(4, 1) prior, rescaled to the ρ scale; blue histograms show draws from the joint prior sampled with blavaan (prisamp = TRUE). Second, one can accept an uninformative Beta(1, 1) prior for the relevant correlation(s), which propagates to an uninformative LKJ(1) on the corresponding block; this maintains a neutral baseline while letting blavaan enforce positive definiteness through a coherent joint prior on the block.

Landscape Analysis

A Bayes factor compares two models. It is conditional on the model set and does not show whether either model fits the data at all. To check this, we use a landscape analysis (Navarro et al., 2004) with the data-informed parametric bootstrap cross-fitting method of Wagenmakers et al. (2004), a global fit check placed on the scale of the Bayes factor. We fit each model to the data by maximum likelihood and generate datasets from each fitted model's implied covariance matrix by parametric bootstrap. Each generated dataset is scored by its BIC-approximated log marginal likelihood under both models, which gives one cloud of points per model in the plane of the two log marginal likelihoods. The observed data are then located in this plane. Data inside the clouds are reproduced by the models; data far outside both clouds are not, whatever Bayes factor they yield. In contrast to Wagenmakers et al. (2004), we do not refit the models to nonparametric bootstrap samples of the data to carry parameter uncertainty into the generating models, and we score the generated datasets by the BIC approximation of the log marginal likelihood instead of the maximum likelihood.

We apply the analysis to the proxy data and the two models of Extension I; the result is shown in Figure 5. Both models are specified as in Extension I and fitted with lavaan

Appendix A Technical Details Bridge Sampling Requirements: Mean Structure and Monitored Parameters

For marginal-likelihood estimation using bridge sampling, the likelihood evaluated by bridgesampling must match the likelihood used inside the fitted blavaan/Stan model. When meanstructure = FALSE, blavaan may switch to a covariance-based likelihood (Wishart, when available) for computational efficiency, whereas other parts of the workflow (including the log-likelihood evaluation used by bridgesampling) may still assume a multivariate-normal likelihood. To avoid this mismatch, all models intended for bridge sampling were fit with meanstructure = TRUE.

In addition, bridge sampling requires access to internal parameter blocks that are not stored in the default blavaan MCMC output. We therefore use blavaan's mcmcextra option to explicitly monitor the additional internal variables needed for log-likelihood evaluation. Monitoring these variables increases memory usage, so we treat this as an opt-in setting for bridge-sampling workflows rather than a default for all Bayesian SEM fits. The exact list of monitored variables and the corresponding blavaan call are provided in the accompanying Zenodo repository (see the varsForMonitor function in the functionsAll.R file at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23397657).

Correlation-Matrix Priors and LKJ Blocks

In SEMs with free latent (residual) correlations, prior specification must respect the requirement that the implied correlation matrix is positive definite. Assigning independent beta priors to individual correlations is convenient and interpretable, but such marginal specifications need not correspond to any coherent joint prior over a correlation matrix. In particular, independently sampled correlations can violate positive definiteness, especially when multiple correlations are free within the same block.

To address this, recent versions of blavaan may replace beta priors on individual free correlations with an LKJ (Lewandowski-Kurowicka-Joe) prior on any unrestricted correlation-matrix block (Lewandowski et al., 2009). The LKJ prior is defined directly on correlation matrices and therefore guarantees positive definiteness by construction. Operationally, if a set of correlations forms a block in which all off-diagonal elements are by maximum likelihood to the standardized proxy data (std.lv = TRUE, indicator means fixed at zero). From each fitted model, we draw 1,000 datasets of N = 500 observations from the multivariate normal distribution with the model-implied covariance matrix and standardize each dataset, as was done for the proxy data. Every generated dataset is then refitted by maximum likelihood under both models, and its log marginal likelihood is approximated by -BIC/2, where BIC is the value reported by lavaan. Datasets for which either model did not converge were discarded (4.6% of those generated from M 0 and 1.6% of those generated from M 1 ). The proxy data are scored in the same way. For each model, we report the share of the datasets generated from it whose log marginal likelihood under that model does not exceed that of the proxy data.

The check assesses the covariance structure. Because the multivariate normal likelihood depends on the data only through the sample means and covariances, it detects data whose covariance matrix neither model can reproduce, but not non-normality that leaves the covariance matrix unchanged. With 1,000 bootstrap datasets per model, the analysis took about 7 minutes on the same computer as in Extension I, and the code is provided in the Zenodo repository.

Here O(1) denotes a bounded term that does not depend on sample size N (i.e., it remains of constant order as N → ∞). Consequently, the BIC approximation can be accurate in large samples while still differing from the exact log Bayes factor by a non-negligible constant in finite samples. In nested models, this constant is often less consequential, and the approximation is typically better behaved; see, for example, discussions in the asymptotic Bayes-factor literature (e.g.,Kass & Wasserman, 1995).

The JAGS backend of blavaan allows more direct custom prior specifications, including truncation, but in the present paper we use the Stan backend because it is faster and integrates naturally with our bridge-sampling workflow.

Deviating from the original study, we removed Sex as a covariate for ease of interpretation and simplicity.

This gain can be substantial. Heuristically, with k focal parameters, correct directional restrictions can increase the Bayes factor by about 2 k , and halving the prior standard deviation can yield a similar gain when the true effects are small (e.g.,MacKay, 2003; Trotta, 2008). Under favorable conditions, the combined effect can therefore approach 4 k.

Under factor-variance scaling, one loading per factor is constrained to be positive for identification. Consequently, an apparently symmetric prior such as N (0, σ 2 ) on that loading is interpreted as a truncated normal prior on the positive half-line (seeMerkle et al., 2023, for discussion of how such implicit constraints can affect prior interpretation). In the present application, this sign constraint is applied consistently across candidate models and we focus on priors for the structural relations, which are not subject to such truncation.
